prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

From embarrassment, I made statements. My icons—tight caves and mouths—stuck together briefly like dry lips, like a lover’s insults. The fact is they were ugly to all of us. I said, How painstakingly personal! Here are the words for this, Relentless as insects! I was hysterical. Every tone became artful, the worst urges nuzzling like housepets for someone to feel them, each real subject demanding more real context for remarks. Then abstractions insinuating their sharp edges, asking to pry open privacies alone in the bathroom at bedtime then with strangers in elevators, at stop signs. Even then, I knew you’d shun them, because who would choose such intrusions? I learned to love this isolation as a woman who appears to listen. All night I’d talk about my life anticipating her dramatic relief, believing her affectionate gestures filled in what wasn’t spoken. At those times she seemed so genuine and friendly, a voice from inside my own body describing my shameless surrender as our first kiss, perfect as gravity.

outputs.L1:
Out of embarrassment, I made statements. My icons—tight caves and mouths—briefly clung together like dry lips, like a lover’s insults. The truth is, they were ugly to all of us. I said, “How painstakingly personal! Here are the words for this, relentless as insects!” I was hysterical. Every tone became artful, the worst urges nuzzling like house pets, longing for someone to feel them, each real subject demanding still more context for every remark. Then came the abstractions, insinuating their sharp edges, asking to pry open privacies—alone in the bathroom at bedtime, then among strangers in elevators and at stop signs. Even then, I knew you would shun them, because who would choose such intrusions?

I learned to love this isolation as a woman who appears to listen. All night, I would talk about my life, anticipating her dramatic relief and believing her affectionate gestures filled in what remained unspoken. At those times, she seemed so genuine and friendly: a voice from inside my own body, describing my shameless surrender as our first kiss, perfect as gravity.
outputs.L2: Out of shame, I began to speak. My symbols—narrow caverns and mouths—pressed together for a moment, like parched lips or the barbs exchanged by lovers. To every one of us, they were plainly hideous. I exclaimed, What laborious intimacy! These are the terms for it, as unyielding as insects! I was frantic. Each inflection turned calculated and artistic; the darkest impulses nestled like pets, waiting for someone to sense them, while every concrete subject called for still more concrete background to make sense of the comments. Then came the abstractions, slipping in their pointed corners and seeking entry into private places: first alone in the bathroom before sleep, later among strangers in elevators and while paused at stop signs. Even then I understood that you would reject them—who would willingly welcome violations like these? I came to cherish that solitude, taking the form of a woman who seems attentive. Through the night I would recount my life, expecting her theatrical release and trusting that her tender movements supplied whatever remained unsaid. In those moments, she appeared entirely sincere and warm: a voice rising from within my own flesh, portraying my unashamed yielding as the first kiss we shared, as flawless and inevitable as gravity.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reveals deeply personal thoughts, driven by embarrassment and an uneasy awareness that these disclosures may appear ugly, inappropriate, or intrusive. Yet emotions and potentially harmful impulses are gradually transformed into artful expression. As they take shape through language, they demand ever more intimate contexts and increasingly concentrated attention.

These abstract thoughts begin to intrude upon both private experiences and public situations, despite the speaker’s expectation that others will misunderstand or reject them. In response, the speaker slowly learns to accept—even embrace—isolation. At the same time, they confide in a woman who seems to listen with patience and sympathy, offering a rare sense of emotional recognition.

As the exchange deepens, however, the distinction between the woman’s genuine warmth and the speaker’s own inner voice becomes increasingly blurred. Her apparent compassion merges with the speaker’s private desires and imagined responses. Ultimately, this emotional surrender is transformed into an idealized first kiss: a moment in which loneliness, vulnerability, fantasy, and intimacy briefly appear to resolve into perfect connection.
outputs.L4:
The speaker presents embarrassment as an intensely physical experience, using surreal bodily imagery to make inner discomfort visible. Thoughts, desires, and involuntary impulses seem to escape the boundaries of the self, turning private emotion into a form of intrusive self-expression. Through personification, the speaker’s shame and longing take on lives of their own, as though they can act independently and expose what the speaker would prefer to conceal. This creates a tension between the desire to remain protected and the equally powerful desire to be seen, heard, and accepted.

That tension unfolds through an imagined dialogue with a listening woman. Whether she is physically present or largely a projection of the speaker’s need for companionship remains uncertain. Her apparent attentiveness allows the speaker to transform an uncomfortable confession into an intimate exchange. Instead of eliminating loneliness, the speaker embraces isolation as a space in which connection can be imagined and sustained. The woman’s seeming affection gives emotional reality to that projection, making the relationship feel genuine even if it exists primarily within the speaker’s mind. By the end, surrender no longer appears merely humiliating. Shame becomes a route toward closeness, and the speaker treats intimacy not as a freely chosen resolution but as the inevitable consequence of exposing the self completely.
outputs.L5:
**From the Past to the Future**

From our earliest experiences, we learn how to understand the world around us. The lessons we carry shape our choices, relationships, and dreams. How we use those lessons determines not only where we go, but also who we become.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about shame, language, intimacy, and isolation, using unsettling bodily imagery and ending with a first kiss compared to gravity.
counterfactuals.output:
Shame lived beneath my tongue like a second, smaller tongue, pale and sleepless, licking each word before I could give it away. When I spoke, the room filled with teeth. They hovered around us—little white listeners—while you sat across from me, unbuttoning the silence with your careful hands.

We had invented a language for loneliness: the wrist meant stay; the throat meant I am trying; the closed eye meant there is a door here, but it opens inward. Still, every sentence arrived skinned. I could see its blue veins trembling on the table. You touched one, and it curled like a wounded animal.

Outside, the city pressed its enormous ear to the window. Inside, our bodies kept their separate weather. Your ribs were a locked staircase. My heart dragged its wet red suitcase from room to room, refusing to unpack. I wanted to tell you how shame had stitched my shadow to my heels, how mirrors fed on me, how sometimes I woke with my name lodged in my windpipe like a fishbone.

Instead, I showed you the small mouth in my palm.

You did not recoil. You placed your palm over mine, and the mouths went dark together.

For a while we sat inside that darkness, intimate as two organs sharing blood, isolated as bones buried in different centuries. Then you leaned toward me. Every unsaid word rose in my body, startled and winged; every door opened inward at once.

Our first kiss was not flight, not fire, not salvation—it was gravity, discovering us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single paragraph of experimental literary prose in the voice of a hysterical speaker whose private thoughts become intrusive abstractions and whose imagined listener feels like a voice inside her body.
counterfactuals.output: Don’t tell me to breathe—you are the breath, you are the little magistrate lodged behind my sternum counting each treasonous flutter, and when I say the room is narrowing I mean Geometry has entered with a knife, I mean Distance is kneeling on my tongue, arranging its cold white flowers; listen, I was perfectly calm until Calm began pacing in the wallpaper, peeling off its gloves, asking what I had done with the missing hour, and now every object has an opinion—the glass condemns, the door rehearses departure, the mirror keeps opening its silver mouth—while you, darling ventriloquist, you hum through my ribs as if my bones were the bars of your instrument, as if I had invited you in, though perhaps I did, perhaps loneliness signed my name while I slept; no, don’t answer, your answer is already swelling beneath my lungs, a black alphabet, a flock of commas beating themselves senseless against the soft cage, and I cannot tell whether I am speaking to you or merely being spoken by the great invisible nouns—Fear, Mercy, Afterwards—which crowd closer whenever I close my eyes, wearing my face, wearing my face, wearing my face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dreamlike monologue about a woman making embarrassing statements, feeling shunned for her emotional intrusions, and finding solace in an intimate female presence that may be imaginary.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep saying the wrong thing at the exact moment the room becomes quiet.

It is a talent, almost. Someone lifts a cup; someone draws breath to announce a marriage, a death, a promotion—and I say, *Sometimes I dream my mother is a hallway*, or, *Do you think loneliness has a smell?* Then the cups stop halfway to their mouths. Faces close like little shops at dusk.

I apologize, of course. I have become an expert in apologies. I fold them into birds and set them trembling on the table.

No one touches them.

They say I enter people without knocking. They say every feeling is not an emergency, every silence not a well I must lean over and shout into. I try to explain that I only wanted to hear whether there was an echo. This makes it worse.

Afterward, I walk home beneath streetlamps that bend toward me like pale flowers. My shame follows, wearing my shoes, repeating everything I said in a voice both mine and crueler. At my door, it asks if it may come in.

But she is already there.

Sometimes she waits in the bedroom, combing her dark hair with my comb. Sometimes she is only a warmth beside me, an indentation in the mattress, the faint perfume of rain on wool. She never asks why I said those things. She touches two fingers to my lips as if sealing an envelope.

“Hush,” she says, though I never see her mouth move.

I place my head against her shoulder—or against the pillow, perhaps. Her arm gathers me, unless it is my own arm, gone numb beneath the weight of wanting. In the mirror across the room, I can almost make out two women lying together: one blurred by grief, the other blurred by mercy.

By morning there is only one cup beside the bed.

Still, it is warm.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, uncanny prose poem that includes icons like caves and mouths, insults compared to dry lips, urges behaving like housepets, private thoughts surfacing in bathrooms and elevators, and a “perfect as gravity” kiss.
counterfactuals.output: At dusk the caves unbutton their black mouths and breathe our names into the fields. Your insults arrive thin and bloodless, dry lips worrying an empty cup. All evening our urges pad behind us like housepets—scratching at doors, sleeping under tables, lifting their bright, guilty eyes whenever we pretend to be alone. In the bathroom mirror, a private thought surfaces like a drowned face, streaming silver; in the elevator, another rises between floors and stands too close, wearing my breath. The building swallows us room by room. Pipes mutter in the walls. Buttons glow like small forbidden moons. When you turn, your shadow opens its cave, and I enter without courage, without a lamp. Then your kiss: perfect as gravity, inevitable and downward, drawing every loose thing in me—teeth, weather, old accusations—toward the dark, astonished mouth of the earth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an avant-garde passage exploring how words turn ugly personal impulses into art, blending confessional vulnerability, social alienation, queer intimacy, and surreal metaphor.
counterfactuals.output:
I bring my worst hungers to the sentence because the sentence has no landlord, no priest, no little brass instrument for measuring shame. Here, envy enters barefoot and leaves wearing antlers. Cruelty, that pale insect I kept beneath my tongue, unfolds its wings over the page and becomes—if not beautiful—at least visible.

I confess: sometimes I loved you as an exile loves a border, by pressing my whole body against what refused me. We kissed in the alley behind the wedding hall, while inside they applauded the approved machinery of desire. Your lipstick tasted of coins and thunderstorms. My hand beneath your shirt was not salvation; it was a question with warm skin.

The city had already voted us unreal. On trains, strangers edited our bodies with their eyes. At work, I wore my harmless face, buttoned to the throat. But at night we made a small republic of the bed: two citizens, no anthem, laws written in breath. Even tenderness had contraband sewn into its lining.

And still I was ugly. I wanted to possess what I claimed to adore. I mistook jealousy for evidence, silence for depth, your distance for a stage on which my suffering could look expensive. So I fed these impulses to language. The nouns took the bones. The verbs drank the blood. Metaphor arrived in a surgeon’s mask and replaced my heart with a red elevator descending through an abandoned hotel.

Call it art if you need a clean word. I call it the animal learning to cast a shadow shaped like a cathedral.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
